prompt.context: Our client is a private equity firm interested in PlasticWorld, a plastic packaging manufacturer. PlasticWorld's owners are requesting $25M. The offer is final.
prompt.question: Should our client buy PlasticWorld for $25M?

clarifying_info.a: Plastic packaging for beverages, cosmetics, household and automotive chemicals.
Products are top quality. They have 350 sets of molds with different materials, finish, and colors, and they are always innovating.

clarifying_info.q: Has the product mix changed recently?
clarifying_info.a: No, the overall product mix has not changed in recent years.

clarifying_info.q: How is the sales force structured and compensated?
clarifying_info.a: The sales force is considered 'the best in breed.' They hold market share and are compensated based on market share.

clarifying_info.q: What is the customer base like?
clarifying_info.a: PlasticWorld's customers exhibit strong loyalty. They are experiencing increasing pressures in their industries to innovate plastic packaging.

clarifying_info.q: Have there been any recent capital investments?
clarifying_info.a: Two years ago they invested further in equipment for product innovation.

clarifying_info.q: Can I see competitor profitability data?

exhibits.title: PlasticWorld P&L Statement (2007–2009)
exhibits.shows: A three-year income statement for PlasticWorld covering 2007, 2008, and 2009.

exhibits.title: PlasticWorld and Industry Peers Profit Margins
exhibits.shows: A bar chart showing profit margin percentages for Competitors A through F and PlasticWorld.

data.note: All competitors appear to have positive profit margins; PlasticWorld appears to be the only one with a negative margin.

exhibits.title: PlasticWorld Valuation Sensitivity Analysis
exhibits.shows: A line or scatter chart mapping profit margin (x-axis, -10% to +15%) to company valuation (y-axis, $0M to $50M).

framework: Assess current financial performance: calculate profit margin, identify revenue and cost trends
Diagnose root cause of declining profitability: pricing vs. cost vs. mix
Benchmark against industry: determine if problem is company-specific or industry-wide
Value the company at current and improved profit margins using sensitivity analysis
Identify feasible operational improvements to lift profitability above the break-even threshold
Formulate buy/no-buy recommendation and post-acquisition improvement plan

questions.prompt: Based on Exhibit 1, what observations can you make and what is the current profit margin?
questions.guidance: Candidate should: (1) Calculate 2009 profit margin = EBIT / Sales = -$1,176,000 / $18,824,000 ≈ -6%. (2) Notice sales volume is growing (32.75M → 36.2M units) while revenues are falling ($19.65M → $18.82M), implying prices per unit are dropping. (3) Note the jump in depreciation from $2.25M (2007) to $3.45M (2008–2009) linked to the equipment investment. (4) Conclude the main driver of negative EBIT is declining revenue per unit, not rising costs.

steps: Price has dropped ~13% while volume grew ~11%
math.answer: 2009 profit margin ≈ -6%; revenue decline is driven by falling price per unit, not falling volume.

questions.prompt: What could explain the drop in prices? (Investigate root cause)
questions.guidance: Candidate should explore: (1) Is it competitive pressure? — Products are high quality and customers are loyal, so price competition is unlikely to be the main driver. (2) Is it customer-driven discounting? — Customers are loyal and do not appear to be switching. (3) Is it sales force behavior? — Sales force is compensated on market share, not profits. This incentivizes reps to cut prices to win/hold volume, directly causing revenue per unit to decline without management necessarily realizing it. Candidate should independently ask about or identify the sales force compensation structure.

questions.prompt: Using Exhibit 2, is the profitability problem company-specific or industry-wide?
questions.guidance: All competitors (A–F) show positive profit margins while PlasticWorld is the only one with a negative margin. This confirms the problem is company-specific, not a sector-wide pricing or cost issue. Candidate should then ask what a realistic profit margin target would be for PlasticWorld based on the industry data (peers range roughly 5–12%, implying ~10% as a reasonable target).

questions.prompt: Using Exhibit 3, at what profit margin is PlasticWorld worth $25M, and what is it worth at the industry average?
questions.guidance: Candidate should read off the sensitivity chart: at 0% profit margin, valuation ≈ $25M (break-even on the deal). At industry-average margin (~10%), valuation ≈ $40M. Therefore the deal is attractive only if profitability can be lifted from -6% to at least 0%, and there is significant upside to ~$40M if industry-average margins are achieved.

math.setup: Read directly from Exhibit 3 sensitivity curve
steps: At profit margin = 0%: company value ≈ $25M (equals the ask price)
At profit margin = 10% (industry avg): company value ≈ $40M
Required improvement: +6 percentage points to break even on deal price
Full upside improvement: +16 percentage points to reach $40M
math.answer: Break-even on the $25M purchase requires lifting margin to 0%; achieving industry-average (~10%) would make the company worth ~$40M.

questions.prompt: What specific changes could PlasticWorld make to improve profitability, and are they feasible?
questions.guidance: Two primary levers: (1) Change sales force compensation from market-share-based to earnings/profit-based — easy to implement, directly removes the incentive to cut prices, likely the fastest win. (2) Simplify the product line — 350 molds is a very dense product line; eliminating lower-value molds reduces complexity costs, but must be balanced against customer pressure for packaging innovation. Candidate should assess feasibility: the sales comp change is straightforward; product line rationalization requires analysis of which molds drive revenue vs. cost. Other improvement areas: examine industry best practices for additional cost reductions.

brainstorming.prompt: What other operational or strategic improvements might a PE acquirer consider to further boost PlasticWorld's value post-acquisition?

categories.name: Pricing & Revenue
ideas: Re-price products upward given high customer loyalty and quality positioning
Introduce tiered pricing for premium vs. standard molds
Negotiate longer-term contracts to stabilize revenue

categories.name: Sales Force
ideas: Shift compensation to profit or EBITDA-based incentives
Add minimum price floors to sales force deal authority
Retrain sales team on value-based selling

categories.name: Product Line & Innovation
ideas: Rationalize 350 molds — discontinue slow-moving or low-margin SKUs
Focus innovation spend on high-demand packaging categories (e.g., sustainable materials)
License or co-develop new packaging designs with key customers to share R&D cost

categories.name: Cost Structure
ideas: Review COGS for purchasing or manufacturing efficiencies
Benchmark SG&A against peers to identify overhead reductions
Optimize depreciation schedule on new equipment

categories.name: Customer Strategy
ideas: Leverage loyalty to upsell higher-margin custom designs
Pursue long-term supply agreements to reduce churn risk
Selectively pass innovation costs through to customers given their strong loyalty

recommendation: Accept the $25M offer — the deal is at fair value today (company worth ~$25M at 0% margin) with clear and actionable upside.

Post-acquisition, the PE firm should immediately implement two high-impact, low-complexity changes: (1) Shift sales force compensation from market-share-based to profit-based, removing the incentive to cut prices; (2) Rationalize the 350-mold product line to reduce complexity costs while maintaining customer satisfaction via the strong sales force.
If these changes bring PlasticWorld to industry-average margins (~10%), the company could be worth ~$40M, representing a ~$15M value creation opportunity.
risks: Sales force turnover or resistance if compensation structure changes abruptly
Customer dissatisfaction if product line rationalization eliminates molds they rely on
Ongoing innovation pressure from customers may require sustained R&D investment that offsets cost savings
Execution risk: reaching industry-average margins requires multiple simultaneous changes
next_steps: Model out detailed impact of sales comp change on revenue per unit and EBIT
Conduct SKU-level profitability analysis to identify which molds to retire
Survey key customers on minimum product line requirements before rationalizing
Benchmark SG&A and COGS against competitors to find additional improvement levers
